metadata.title: UDL Quick Start: Multiple Means of Action & Expression
metadata.summary: A ~15-minute primer on the action and expression principle of Universal Design for Learning: accessible interaction, multiple ways to show knowledge, and strategy-development supports, with a knowledge check and an action step. Aligned to the CAST UDL Guidelines 3.0 (2024).

activities.title: Separate the goal from the route to it

content.body:
The action and expression principle of Universal Design for Learning — the 'how' of learning — starts from a simple observation: knowing something and producing a particular kind of performance about it are not the same skill. A learner can understand a historical argument and still struggle to handwrite five paragraphs about it; the handwriting is not the goal. UDL asks teachers to be precise about what the goal actually is, then flexible about the routes learners take to demonstrate it. The guideline names below are from the CAST UDL Guidelines 3.0 (2024), with the older 2.2 names for reference.

Interaction (Guideline 4; formerly Physical Action) is the access layer: can every learner operate the materials and tools? This includes navigation, response options that do not depend on one motor skill, and compatibility with assistive technologies. When the response method is the barrier, the assessment measures the barrier, not the learning.

Expression and communication (Guideline 5) is the heart of the principle: offer multiple media for composition — writing, speaking, drawing, building, recording — and provide the construction tools professionals actually use, such as spellcheckers, speech-to-text, sentence starters, and models of strong work. Support matters most while fluency is developing; the guideline calls for graduated levels of support that fade as independence grows.

Strategy development (Guideline 6; formerly Executive Functions) recognizes that producing work requires planning, organizing, remembering, and monitoring — capacities that are still developing throughout childhood and adolescence. Goal-setting supports, planning templates, checklists that offload working memory, and structured opportunities to monitor progress make the difference between a learner who knows and a learner who can show it.

One caution keeps this honest: when a specific mode IS the goal — a writing standard, an oral defense — then that mode is not negotiable, and UDL instead asks how to scaffold every learner toward it.
keyPoints: Be precise about the goal; be flexible about the route to demonstrating it.
Access first: the response method must not be the barrier (Guideline 4, Interaction).
Offer multiple composition media and real construction tools, with supports that fade (Guideline 5).
Strategy-development supports — plans, checklists, progress monitoring — turn knowing into showing (Guideline 6).
When the mode itself is the standard, scaffold toward it rather than around it.

questions.prompt: The core move of the action and expression principle is to:
options: Let every student decide for themselves whether to complete the assignment at all
Hold the learning goal constant while allowing multiple routes to demonstrate it
Replace every writing task in the course with an oral presentation of equal length
Grade the effort a student visibly puts in rather than the product they turn in
questions.explanation: The goal stays fixed; the route to demonstrating it flexes — unless the mode itself is the standard.

questions.prompt: A student uses speech-to-text to draft an essay analyzing a novel's theme. The learning goal is literary analysis. This is best described as:
options: An unfair advantage over classmates who typed their drafts
A reason to grade the essay on a separate rubric from the class
Lowering the standard of the assignment because the student did not type it
Removing a barrier so the assessment measures the actual goal
questions.explanation: Transcription was not the goal. When the response method is the barrier, the task measures the barrier.

questions.prompt: Which is a STRATEGY DEVELOPMENT support (Guideline 6) rather than an expression option?
options: A project checklist with milestones the student checks off against dates
Allowing a recorded podcast episode instead of a poster for the final product
Providing colored markers and poster board for students who prefer to draw
Reading the rubric aloud to the class before the project is assigned
questions.explanation: Planning and progress-monitoring tools offload executive demands; media choice is Guideline 5.

questions.prompt: The state writing standard requires a persuasive ESSAY. The UDL-consistent response is to:
options: Let students who dislike writing film a persuasive video instead of writing the essay
Excuse students who find writing difficult from the essay and assess them on participation
Scaffold every learner toward the essay — models, sentence frames, dictation for drafting, graduated support
Have students copy a model essay by hand, sentence by sentence, so they experience what a strong persuasive essay looks like
questions.explanation: When the mode is the goal, UDL scaffolds toward it. Options and supports serve the standard, not a detour around it.

content.prompt: Take one assessment you already use. State its actual learning goal in one sentence. Then name one part of the required performance that is NOT the goal (handwriting, spelling under time pressure, oral fluency, recall of directions) and one route or support you could offer without touching the goal itself.
